extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, public administrators, political scientists, reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and institutional criteria for organizing governmental intelligence/research bureaus and for structuring procedures by which expert information is brought to bear on public decisions and appeals to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of knowledge-assembly and policy control
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the assembling of knowledge (experts) distinct from the control of policy (decision-makers); experts must not meddle in decisions or display a partisan 'policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: experts who take sides are soon discounted because caring too much biases perception; example contrasts British embassies' discounting of wartime mind with an American ambassador who only reported things that cheered folks at home (anti-pattern). The expert's power depends on not caring which decision is made; institutional arrangements should preserve this separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert reports must translate the environment faithfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts should 'bring the Far East to the Secretary's desk' — translate, simplify, and generalize so that inferences apply to the external environment, not merely to the premises of the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports must represent different classes' beliefs and likely actions; the aim is fidelity and applicability to the real situation, not advocacy for a policy position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts represent unseen/intonigible constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts' constituency is 'intangibles' — mute people, unborn people, relations and functions not otherwise represented in politics; they represent matters not forming an immediate material majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legitimizes expert influence: by making invisible facts visible they can reshape the environment and thereby affect decisions without being partisan actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute separation of investigative staff and executing staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff which executes (managers, superintendents, foremen) must be separate and parallel to staff which investigates (auditors, accountants, inspectors); recruit and structure them differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should be distinct bodies of men, recruited differently, paid (if possible) from separate funds, responsible to different heads, and intrinsically uninterested in each other's personal success to avoid capture and bureaucratic aggregation of decision power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from departmental and congressional control
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence officials should be independent of the Congressional Committees dealing with that department and of the Secretary at the head of it; they must not be entangled in decision or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence hinges on three practical points: funds, tenure, and access to facts. If Congress or departmental officials can remove money, dismiss staff, or close files, independence is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure and protected funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Research agencies must have financial arrangements insulating them from arbitrary annual appropriations or petty attacks—funding should be entrenched and provide for growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested mechanisms: a federal charter creating a trust fund that covers minimum overhead and capital charges, plus a sliding scale tied to departmental appropriations for expansions; appropriation should be 'put beyond accident' so attacks require open repeal rather than surreptitious undermining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable professional tenure with protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure for intelligence staff should be for life with liberal pension provisions, sabbaticals for study and training, and dismissal only after trial by professional colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conditions consistent with non-profit intellectual careers so that staff have dignity, security, and freedom of mind necessary for salient investigative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed access to materials and questioning rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The bureau should have statutory right to examine all papers and to question any official or outsider; access to materials should be established in the organic act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous investigation should be nondramatic (distinct from sensational inquiries); the bureau should be able to propose accounting methods to the department and, if rejected or violated, appeal under its charter to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureau as connecting link between legislature and department
rubrics_metrics.description: Each intelligence bureau should function as the Congressional eye on departmental execution and as the departmental answer to Congressional criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visibility may reduce need for minute legislation and make administration more efficient by making operations permanently visible to both Congress and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable standards and exchange of records for coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Different bureaus should adopt wherever possible comparable standards of measurement and exchange their records to enable meaningful comparison and competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable measures let departments treat similar purchases or operations competitively and support coordination without excessive centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent and use quantitative indices for desired goals
rubrics_metrics.description: To direct competition toward social ends, develop index numbers or quantitative measures for the qualities and objectives you wish to promote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better index numbers enable comparisons across workers, shops, factories, schools, departments, regiments, cities, states, etc.; examples cited include index numbers for state school systems and quota systems like Liberty Loan campaigns. (Author notes 'index numbers' is used broadly as any device for comparative measurement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Central clearing house/central agency to aggregate and reshape information
rubrics_metrics.description: A central clearing house should assemble facts in forms suited to decision problems and serve as a focus of extraordinary information and social-scientific technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a body would handle problems of definition, terminology, statistical technique and logic, and could form the makings of a national university that supplies staff and specialists to bureaus and trains researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation of personnel and data between agencies and academia
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure circulation of men, data, and criticism among government departments, industry, and universities, including temporary specialist appointments and exchange lecturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation mitigates risks of ossification and dry rot, integrates training and recruitment, and prevents the bureaus from becoming isolated pedantic fiefdoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and federated coordination of bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the intelligence-bureau principle to states, cities, and counties via federations and desirable regional combinations so that comparable accounting avoids duplication and reconciles autonomy with cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legal frontiers often don't match functional environments, coordinated information allows municipalities to see common problems in the same light (example: metropolitan functions like health and transportation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design against bureaucratic degeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the risk that intelligence networks could become red tape—attracting soft jobs, pedants, meddlers, producing mountains of paper and procedural absurdities—and design institutions to avoid this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate risks through circulation of personnel, open exchange of data and criticism, and by keeping bureaus connected with the practitioners who use the intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary focus on aiding responsible decision-makers, not burdening citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence systems should primarily serve men of action—representatives charged with decision, workers at their work—not aim to make every citizen an expert on every subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bureau's real use is to assist representative government and administration; public access and press-checks are secondary. Do not assume the general public can digest expert documents routinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public can (and should) judge procedure and results, not technical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The general public can typically judge whether procedures were proper (were groups heard, ballots honest, process accepted) and judge results after the event, but cannot determine technical relevance of facts in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grounds a standard that appeals to public opinion should focus on procedural legitimacy; outsiders should demand proper procedure rather than trying to substitute lay judgment for expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement: issues should pass expert-driven procedure before public appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should not be raised to the public until they have passed through a procedure in which representatives debate in the presence of a chairman/mediator who forces reliance on expert analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the organization of representative bodies dealing with distant matters: partisans present views, but are confronted by neutral interlocutors who sort real perception from stereotype using available analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference/hearing rules under a neutral chairman with expert access
rubrics_metrics.description: In disputes, convene a conference with a neutral chairman who can call consulting experts for the parties and government, demand empirical evidence (e.g., wage tables), rule on jurisdictional points, and refer technical disputes to standing intelligence bodies when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (steel industry): chairman substitutes wage tables for partisan rhetoric, rules on admissibility of official figures, directs parties to standing intelligence bureaus for appeals, and requires production of private books or issues public statements when claims can't be substantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reporting when private evidence is withheld
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party claims consequences (e.g., 'we shall be ruined') but refuses to produce private evidence, the chairman/public intelligence agency should issue public statements based on available official figures and note the refusal to produce private books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents partisan evasion and ensures transparency; private claims without verifiable evidence do not bind public judgment.
